predecessors.name: Kingdom of the Franks
predecessors.text: Theuderic I's share of Clovis I's kingdom at the partition of 511: 'the lands that were to become Austrasia'

successors.name: Kingdom of the Franks
successors.text: Austrasia, Alemannia and Thuringia, the 741 share of Carloman, passing to Pepin III and the Frankish kingdom

rulers.name: Dagobert I
rulers.title: sub-king of Austrasia (also king of all the Franks from 629)

ledger.x: 511: At Clovis I's death his four sons partition the Frankish kingdom and Theuderic I receives Austrasia, with his capital at Reims.
532: Theuderic I's Franks overthrow the Thuringian kingdom.
555: Theudebald dies and Austrasia is absorbed by Chlothar I.
561: Chlothar I's death gives Sigebert I Austrasia again.
567: Charibert I of Paris dies and his brothers share his lands; Tours and Poitiers are Austrasian by 575 ('took Tours and Poitiers from Austrasia').
575: Sigebert I is assassinated and Chilperic I of Neustria takes Tours and Poitiers from Austrasia, 'along with places in Aquitaine such as Saintes and territory in Auvergne'.
587: By the Treaty of Andelot Guntram, king of Burgundy, cedes Tours to his nephew Childebert II of Austrasia, whom he adopts as heir; Gregory of Tours judged the cession significant.
599: At Dormelles Theuderic II and Theudebert II defeat Chlothar II, whose treaty 'reduced his kingdom to the regions of Beauvais, Amiens and Rouen'; the rest 'was split between' the two brothers.
612: Theuderic II of Burgundy takes Austrasia from his brother Theudebert II (list: Theudebert II 595-612, Theuderic II 612-613).
623: The Austrasians ask for their own king and Chlothar II gives them his son Dagobert I, with Pepin of Landen as regent.
623: Alsace joins Dagobert I's Austrasia: Chlothar II 'excluded Alsace from Dagobert's Austrasia.
629: Dagobert I inherits Neustria and Burgundy and rules the whole realm; the Francia page: in 632 he 'reunited the entire Frankish realm'.
633: Dagobert I gives the Austrasians Sigebert III as sub-king, forced on him by the Austrasian aristocracy.
640: Duke Radulf of Thuringia rebels and defeats Sigebert III, taking Thuringia out of Austrasia.

673: Neustrian and Burgundian magnates invite Childeric II of Austrasia to become king of the whole realm: 'some Neustrian and Burgundian magnates invited Childeric to become king of the whole realm'.
675: After Childeric II's death Theuderic III 'retook his throne' and Dagobert II rules Austrasia (list 675-679).
679: Dagobert II dies and Austrasia passes to Theuderic III: 'When Dagobert II died in 679, Theuderic received Austrasia as well.'
741: Charles Martel's sons divide the realm and Carloman takes Austrasia, Alemannia and Thuringia, Pepin Neustria, Provence and Burgundy.
742: The Duchy of Alsace is dissolved when no successor to the dead Duke Liutfrid is named; Carloman, ruling Austrasia and Alemannia, suppresses the Alemanni 742-746.
751: The infobox ends Austrasia in 751 (Childeric III, last Merovingian king, 743-751; Pepin III mayor 747-751); the term 'Austrasia' was used only occasionally after the Carolingians took power.

wars.name: Frankish conquest of Thuringia
wars.outcome: Theuderic I and his relatives defeat Herminafrid in two battles and take the Unstrut region; Thuringia is Frankish from 531-532.

wars.name: Frankish conquest of the Burgundian kingdom
wars.outcome: 'In 534, Theudebert along with his uncles conquered Burgundy and partitioned it among themselves.'

wars.name: Theudebert I's intervention in Italy
wars.outcome: Theudebert invaded northern Italy in 539 but 'his expedition ended soon and retreated due to supply shortages and disease'; he is said to have kept the Alpine passes and, undated, captured the Cottian Alps, parts of Liguria and most of Venetia, which Totila…

wars.name: Austrasian-Neustrian wars
wars.outcome: 'Neustria and Austrasia fight almost constantly, with Burgundy often mediating' until Chlothar II takes both in 613.

wars.name: Radulf's revolt in Thuringia
wars.outcome: Radulf defeats Sigebert III in 640 and Thuringia leaves Austrasia.

certainty.note: Merovingian partitions are given by cities and rivers, not frontiers; the Rhine, Meuse and Moselle cores are loosely known and the frontiers with the Saxons, Frisians, Alemanni and Bavarians are approximate throughout.
